summary:
Diyarbakır is the largest city of south-east Türkiye and stands under the national legal framework that Human Rights Watch and Kaos GL document as actively hostile to trans people. Official framing around "the family" and "public morals" is the stated basis of that policy, and enforcement has run ahead of legislation that remains unenacted.

Human Rights Watch reported on 29 October 2025 that a leaked draft of Türkiye's 11th Judicial Package would amend penal-code article 225 to punish conduct "contrary to biological sex" with up to three years' imprisonment, and would permit charges against anyone taking part in a same-sex engagement or marriage ceremony carrying up to four years. Under civil-code article 40 the same draft would raise the minimum age for gender-affirming care from 18 to 25 and attach a permanent-infertility mandate, with providers facing fines and up to seven years and patients up to three. Fifteen LGBT organisations and the Turkish Medical Association objected, and Human Rights Watch called for the draft's withdrawal. The measure had not been enacted when reported, but authorities have applied its prohibitions in practice: police in Türkiye's largest city stopped roughly twenty trans women in 2025 for "General Information Gathering" checks, documented them and released them without fines, and foreign visitors stopped at such checkpoints must produce original identity documents, which creates a direct outing risk where appearance does not match the passport gender marker.

Kaos GL's LGBTI+ Human Rights Report 2025, published 24 February 2026 under the title "A Major Siege", finds that hostility became explicit state policy during the year under "Year of the Family" instructions. It documents six right-to-life violations, three of them hate-motivated killings, with trans people the most affected group; 89 torture and ill-treatment violations, up from 51 the previous year; and 313 right-to-liberty violations, roughly two and a half times the previous year and consisting mostly of detentions. Türkiye's state keeps no official hate-crime statistics, so the report's figures rest on media coverage rather than official records.

The national framework also governs custody and care. Trans prisoners are placed according to registered sex rather than gender identity, and a transgender prisoner was found dead at Sincan Women's Prison on 1 December 2025, with rights groups demanding an independent investigation. A Health Ministry regulation reported in September 2025 barred hospitals from recording the "other" option in gender-related e-reports, a change that risks profiling trans patients in official records and restricting access to transition care.
tangentialFactors:
The Istanbul GBT-check episode is cited as an illustration of national street-level practice, not as a Diyarbakır incident. Legal experts quoted in that reporting argue the checks violate Article 5 of the European Convention on Human Rights, and one detainee stated that the new law had not yet been passed even as enforcement was already being applied to her.

Kaos GL states that Türkiye maintains no official hate-crime statistics, so its violation counts derive from media monitoring. Reported totals are therefore a floor rather than a measure of true incidence, and provinces with thinner local reporting may be undercounted relative to Istanbul and Ankara.

The draft judicial package was still pending as of late October 2025. Its unenacted status has not constrained enforcement, and the gap between the written law and street practice is itself a factor for visitors to weigh.

Human Rights Watch's 2008 report We Need a Law for Liberation, based on more than 70 interviews over three years, documented continuing beatings, robberies and abuse against gay men and transgender people. It predates legal changes made after 2018 and is cited as historical evidence of the regime's depth rather than as a statement of current law.
localsOnly:
Residents of Diyarbakır face the same penal-code exposure as the rest of Türkiye. Conduct characterised as "contrary to biological sex" would carry up to three years' imprisonment under the draft article 225, and participation in a same-sex engagement or marriage ceremony would carry up to four years.

Gender-affirming care would be restricted to those aged 25 and over under the draft civil-code article 40, with a permanent-infertility mandate attached; providers would face fines and up to seven years and patients up to three. Fifteen LGBT organisations and the Turkish Medical Association objected to the package.

Kaos GL's 2025 count records 89 torture and ill-treatment violations against the previous year's 51 and 313 right-to-liberty violations, mostly detentions, about two and a half times the prior year. Six right-to-life violations were recorded, three classified as hate-motivated killings, with trans people most affected.

Trans prisoners are held according to registered sex. A transgender prisoner died at Sincan Women's Prison on 1 December 2025, and coordinated branches of the Human Rights Association in Istanbul, Ankara, Izmir, Diyarbakır, Mersin and Aydın demanded an independent investigation; opposition MP Sevda Karaca raised the case in parliament on 12 December 2025.

Because the state keeps no official hate-crime statistics, residents seeking redress rely on media-documented cases and NGO reporting rather than police records.
outOfScopeNotes:
The source inventory records no Diyarbakır-specific enforcement action, arrest, prosecution or violent incident involving a trans person. The province-level picture is unresolved: the two sources are national in scope, and neither contains local policing data for Diyarbakır.

Whether the 11th Judicial Package has been enacted since the Human Rights Watch report of 29 October 2025 is not sourced here. The draft's status should be treated as pending and unverified beyond that date.

Local LGBTI+ organisations, safe venues and healthcare providers operating in Diyarbakır are not covered by these sources; their availability is not sourced rather than absent.

The Kaos GL figures rest on media monitoring, as the report itself states, so province-level incidence in Diyarbakır cannot be derived from them.
